client: I've been really struggling since my grandma passed away last month. At work, I keep zoning out during meetings and forgetting simple tasks, which isn't like me at all. And then out of nowhere, I'll just get hit with this wave of sadness that makes it hard to even pretend I'm okay. I'm not sure talking about it will help - it's not like it'll bring her back.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a deep sense of loss that's affecting both your emotions and your ability to focus at work. While it's understandable to question whether talking can help, grieving is a process that often needs space to unfold—have you noticed any moments when the sadness feels slightly more manageable?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I guess there are moments when I'm distracted by work tasks where the sadness isn't as intense, but then I feel guilty for not thinking about my loss. It's like I can't win - if I think about it I'm overwhelmed, and if I don't I feel like I'm betraying the person I lost. 

People keep telling me the pain will fade with time, but it's been months and I still cry every morning in the shower. Does this really get easier, or do I just get used to feeling broken?
therapist: I hear how torn you feel between honoring your grief and trying to function—that inner conflict sounds exhausting. The way your voice tightens when you talk about this makes me wonder if you're carrying extra weight from judging your own grieving process. Could we explore what your grandmother might say about how you're treating yourself right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know... my grandmother was always so kind and patient with everyone. She'd probably tell me I'm being too hard on myself. But that just makes me feel worse, like I'm failing at grieving "correctly" too. Everyone expects me to be sad but also functional, and I can't seem to do either well right now.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between everyone else's expectations and your own harsh judgments about how grief "should" look—that flatness in your voice tells me how exhausting this struggle has become. Your grandmother's wisdom about kindness might apply here too—what if grieving well simply means allowing yourself to feel exactly what you feel, without grading it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I know logically that grief doesn't have rules, but I still feel guilty when I don't cry at the "right" times. People keep expecting me to fall apart, and when I don't, I worry there's something wrong with me. 

It's easier said than done to just feel what I feel—what if what I'm feeling is numbness? That doesn't seem like proper grieving to me.
therapist: Your voice sounds anxious as you describe this pressure to grieve "correctly"—that rapid pace and higher pitch show how much this weighs on you. Numbness isn't wrong or broken; it's often our mind's way of protecting us when feelings become too overwhelming—have you considered that perhaps your grandma would understand why you might need moments of distance from the pain?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess I hadn't really thought about it that way—that numbness could be protective. It still feels wrong though, like I'm failing her by not feeling more. My family seems so much more emotional, and I keep wondering if they judge me for how I'm handling this. Part of me wants to feel more, but it's like there's this wall I can't get past.
therapist: I can hear the frustration in your voice as you describe this wall—it sounds like you're judging yourself for not grieving the way others are, while also feeling pressured to perform your sadness. That quiet intensity in your words suggests how much this inner conflict is draining you. What if we treated that numbness not as failure, but as your mind's way of pacing this incredibly painful process?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I never thought of the numbness as my mind protecting me... but I guess it makes sense. It's just hard because everyone keeps telling me I should be crying more or talking about my feelings, and when I don't, I feel broken. Like maybe I didn't love them enough if I'm not falling apart the way others are.  

But when you put it that way—that it might be my brain's way of handling the pain—that actually makes me feel a little less guilty. Still, part of me wonders if I'm just avoiding the grief altogether. How do I know if it's protection or just denial?
therapist: The way your voice speeds up and tightens tells me how much this question troubles you—it's like you're holding your breath waiting for the "right" answer about your grief. What if we let go of judging whether it's protection or denial, and simply notice when those quiet moments come? Sometimes simply observing our reactions without grading them can reveal their purpose with time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know... when you say to just observe without judging, it makes me feel like I'm failing at grieving "correctly." Like if I notice the quiet moments but don't analyze them, am I just avoiding the pain? That's what scares me - that I'm either doing this wrong or running away from it. 

The idea of letting go of judging feels impossible right now because the judgment is what keeps me feeling connected to my loss, in a twisted way. If I stop evaluating how I'm grieving, won't that mean I'm forgetting?
therapist: I hear the fear rising in your voice as you describe this—that faster pace and higher pitch show how much this dilemma is gripping you. It makes perfect sense that you'd worry about forgetting when your love runs so deep, but might judging yourself actually be creating more distance from the very connection you're trying to preserve? Could we sit with that idea for a moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don't know... when you put it that way, it makes me feel even more guilty for worrying so much. Like now I'm failing at grieving "correctly" too. It's just that when I start forgetting little things about her, it feels like I'm losing her all over again.
therapist: Your voice sounds so strained as you describe this fear of forgetting—that tension tells me how deeply this worries you. Those small details about your grandmother matter precisely because your love for her was so specific and real—perhaps we could explore ways to honor those memories without the pressure to perfectly preserve them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I know you're right about the love being what matters most, but it still feels terrifying to think those little details might fade. Like if I forget the exact way she used to hum while cooking, it's like losing another piece of her. The idea of "honoring" memories sounds nice, but how do I do that when my brain keeps betraying me by forgetting things?
therapist: Your voice sounds so tender and vulnerable right now—it's clear how precious these memories are to you. That quiet desperation shows how much meaning lives in those small details, but might the fear of forgetting actually be making it harder to hold onto them? What if we explored gentle ways to document those special moments, not as a test of your love, but as an act of kindness to your future self?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying, but writing things down or taking pictures... it feels wrong somehow. Like I'm turning something sacred into just another item on a checklist. What if documenting it actually makes the memory feel less special? I already worry so much about not remembering things perfectly.
therapist: Your voice sounds softer and more hesitant now, carrying that thoughtful concern about preserving what feels sacred. It makes sense that you'd worry about losing the special quality of these memories—that gentle resistance tells me how deeply you cherish them. What if we thought about documentation not as a checklist, but as a way to create little gifts for yourself to rediscover later?
